episodes.209889: A warm front lifted north across eastern North Carolina during the morning hours of February twentieth which allowed for a warm, moist, and unstable airmass to set up across portions of North Carolina during the late morning and afternoon hours. At the same time, a cold front located across the Appalachians during the morning hours quickly pushed east across North Carolina and across the area waters during the afternoon of February twentieth. Along and just out ahead of this frontal boundary, a broken line of showers and thunderstorms developed. With a somewhat favorable environment in place, a few isolated storms became strong in nature bringing strong and damaging wind gusts to portions of the inland rivers and sounds of eastern North Carolina during the afternoon hours.
episodes.209905: A frontal boundary sank into the area on the 19th of February and then remained in the vicinity as a low-pressure system moved northeast into the Great Lakes region. The boundary became occluded overhead before being ushered northeast out of the area by the parent low on the 20th. Meanwhile, a cold front approached from the west and then washed out as it moved through the middle Ohio Valley later in the day. Although isolated showers skimmed across southeast Ohio on the 19th, more robust showers and storms did not arrive until late that night. A few strong to severe storms that developed overnight produced gusty winds and penny size hail. The majority of activity shifted east across the Ohio River before daybreak on the 20th, then drier conditions took hold for the rest of the day. Rainfall amounts for this event generally totaled around an inch or less.
episodes.209906: A frontal boundary sank into the Central Appalachians on the 19th of February and then remained in the vicinity as a low-pressure system moved northeast into the Great Lakes region. The boundary became occluded overhead before being ushered northeast out of the area by the parent low on the 20th. Meanwhile, a cold front approached from the west and then washed out as it moved through the middle Ohio Valley later in the day.||Isolated to scattered showers and thunderstorms passed across portions of southwest Virginia on the 19th, then a lull occurred that night. A strong line approached from the west early on the 20th and progressed across Buchanan and Dickenson Counties. A couple of downed trees were observed subsequent to the departure of the line, which exited to the east shortly after daybreak. Drier conditions then took hold for the rest of the day. Rainfall amounts for the event generally totaled around an inch or less.
episodes.209907: A frontal boundary sank into the area on the 19th of February and then remained in the vicinity as a low-pressure system moved northeast into the Great Lakes region. The boundary became occluded overhead before being ushered northeast out of the area by the parent low on the 20th. Meanwhile, a cold front approached from the west and then washed out as it moved through the middle Ohio Valley later in the day. The first round of precipitation lifted north across West Virginia the morning of the 19th, then rounds of more robust showers and thunderstorms rolled through the area that afternoon into the night. After a very brief break in activity, more showers and storms spread into the area from the southwest shortly after midnight and then slid east across the mountains by mid-morning on the 20th. Drier conditions then took hold for the rest of the day.||Strong to severe storms downed multiple trees and power lines, and produced hail between one and one-and-three-quarter inches in size. While rainfall amounts of two inches or less were observed across much of the area, portions of the southern coal fields received two to three and a half inches. Excessive rainfall caused flooding on some roads as local creeks, streams, and smaller rivers exceeded their banks in Boone and Logan Counties. A combination of rainfall and snowmelt also prompted minor flooding on Mill Creek in Randolph County.

episodes.210698: A strengthening storm system lifted through the Middle Mississippi Valley on the 19th, dragging its warm frontal zone northward through the Midwest, and bringing near-record high temperatures and anomalous dewpoints into central Indiana.  Multiple rounds of severe weather occurred over the region, from early morning large hail in two far-northern zones, covering roads in Warren County, to more organized evening severe weather from rotating supercell thunderstorms.  Through the evening of the 19th, the destabilized atmosphere combined with a stregthening low-level jet stream that progressed eastward into the region, boosting 0-1 km wind shear as high as 300 m2/s2.  A resultant cluster of discrete late-day to evening supercells were focused along the frontal zone, near or south of the Interstate 70 corridor, and produced scattered large hail over 6 counties and isolated wind damage to trees and/or power poles in 4 counties.  ||A stronger supercell with a history of producing two weak tornadoes in Crawford County, Illinois, continued into central Indiana, spawning an EF-0 tornado in Sullivan County, an intense EF-2 just west of Bloomington that caused extensive structural damage to homes, apartments, and airport facilities, and a brief EF-U in Decatur County;  this cell also produced ping-pong ball (1.50-inch diameter) sized hail in Greene and Monroe Counties.
episodes.210785: A cold front helped force a line of showers and weak thunderstorms that crossed from west to east across East Tennessee. Winds aloft were quite strong, and convective transport in the strongest cells helped bring those winds to the surface in the form of convective downdraft gusts, producing damage and high winds.
episodes.210938: A surface low lifted northeastward across Missouri towards the Illinois-Iowa border during the afternoon and evening of February 19th. A warm front extended east from the low into southeast Illinois. In response to this system, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed across central and southeast Illinois, with the greatest coverage being in the general vicinity of the I-70 corridor. Environmental conditions supported all severe hazards, including large hail up to 2.5 inches in diameter, damaging winds, and tornadoes, with a total of eight tornadoes occurring in the NWS Lincoln coverage area. Most of these tornadoes were brief, and none were stronger than EF-1, but one serious injury occurred in Crawford County as a result of a tornado. Another indirect injury occurred on I-57 in Effingham County when thunderstorm winds contributed to a multi-vehicle accident.
episodes.211361: A dynamic storm system brought unseasonably warm temperatures and rounds of severe weather to eastern Kentucky on February 19th and 20th. Near record warmth, combined with intense wind shear, fueled both discrete supercells and a subsequent overnight line of showers and thunderstorms.||The primary threat focused along the Mountain Parkway corridor during the afternoon of the 19th, where thunderstorms produced up to quarter-sized hail (1.00). As the system's cold front crossed the region overnight, the threat transitioned to isolated damaging winds. High-momentum air mixing to the surface downed trees and utility lines in Lee and Breathitt counties.
episodes.211492: By mid-February, higher moisture content from a lingering front and locally induced afternoon shower and thunderstorm activity produced periods of heavy rainfall across Puerto Rico.
episodes.211509: After a prolonged cold period that allowed for rapid river ice growth, a period of unusual warm temperatures helped to melt and rot the ice. During the melt process, some ice jams were observed along the Allegheny River and other tributaries along the Beaver and Ohio Rivers.

events.narrative: Emergency management reported that an ice jam had broken loose on Oil Creek and was moving downstream toward Oil City where ice was jammed at the mouth of the creek. The water rose rapidly and flooded portions of Seneca Street before all of the ice began moving out of the creek into the Allegheny River.
The Monroe County Airport ASOS gusted to 61KT as the EF2 tornado vortex center tracked 700 yards to the north-northwest.

A tornado developed just south of the Clay-Effingham county line, producing damage at a farmstead along the county line east of 1800th Street. At this location, metal from the top of a silo was blown off, and a barn was damaged with roof pieces blown off to the northeast for about a half mile. The tornado was in Clay County for less than a minute, before continuing northeast into Effingham County. This tornado had a maximum intensity of EF-0, and its total duration was 11 minutes.

A tornado developed just south of the Clay-Effingham county line, producing damage at a farmstead along the county line east of 1800th Street. At this location, metal from the top of a silo was blown off, and a barn was damaged with roof pieces blown off to the northeast for about a half mile. The tornado was in Clay County for less than a minute, before continuing northeast into Effingham County where it produced tracks through corn stubble in fields. It dissipated northwest of the intersection of East 200th Avenue and County Road 2200. This tornado had a maximum intensity of EF-0, and its total lifespan was 11 minutes.

A tornado developed near Scooter Drive in Clay County. It tracked northeast, moving into Effingham County and tracking east of Edgewood. The maximum intensity of this tornado was EF-0, with damage limited to tree branches. The total duration of this tornado was four minutes, one minute in Clay County and three minutes in Effingham County.

A tornado developed near Scooter Drive in Clay County. It tracked northeast, moving into Effingham County and tracking east of Edgewood. It dissipated near the intersection of East 100th Avenue and County Road 880. The maximum intensity of this tornado was EF-0, with damage limited to tree branches. The total duration of this tornado was four minutes, one minute in Clay County and three minutes in Effingham County.
